The programme addresses two main priorities in the region that have been identified during the formulation process – (i) to promote more integrated solutions for climate action that brings benefits across SDGs and for crisis prevention/recovery goals, and (ii) to scale up local partnerships and finance to this end. Through a combination of regional dialogues and technical assistance at the regional level, and innovation grants at the country level, the programme would generate three key outcomes: • Outcome 1: Enhanced knowledge and coordination on climate-security among key stakeholders at the regional level to achieve climate action with co-benefits across the SDGs, and crisis prevention/recovery goals. • Outcome 2: Enhanced access to analysis, tools and strategies at the regional level to support a climate nexus approach to achieving SDGs and prevention/recovery • Outcome 3: Strengthened national and local capacities to effectively integrate climate change considerations into development and crisis prevention/recovery policies and to scale-up climate finance for local innovative solutions with co-benefits across the SDGs Underlying and cutting across these outcomes will be the establishment of SDG-Climate Facility, which will take forward a nexus approach beyond the life-cycle of the project. The programme will focus on the following countries to develop local capacity, deploy integrated solutions and support scale-up of climate financing: Egypt, Iraq, Palestine, Tunisia, Yemen, as well as a response to the Syria crisis in Jordan as a host country of Syrian refugees.

Outcome 1: Enhanced knowledge and coordination on climate security among key stakeholders at the regional level to achieve climate action with cobenefits across the SDGs, and crisis prevention/recovery goals.
Through this outcome, the project aimed to enhance policymakers' and stakeholders' awareness and understanding of how a nexus approach to climate action can generate cobenefits across the SDGs and support crisis prevention and recovery. It also sought to facilitate regional dialogue to identify and prioritize key policy development processes where this approach would have the greatest impact and added value. To achieve this, the project planned to establish a multistakeholder SDG Climate Facility, support regional strategy development, and integrate climate risks into decisionmaking.
It also aimed to strengthen coordination, facilitate policy dialogues, and produce knowledge products to enhance institutional capacity and promote crosssector collaboration. However, this plan was revised to support the LAS in rolling out a Regional Climate Security Initiative. While this shift ensured greater alignment with regional institutional structures, it also delayed establishing a concrete mechanism for sustained coordination. To support institutional coordination, the project supported creating and reinforcing regional networks. Establishing the Regional Climate Security Network (RCSN), initially including 29 member organizations spanning UN agencies, government bodies, research institutions, and NGOs, was a key achievement.
Outcome 2: Enhanced access to analysis, tools, and strategies at the regional level to support a climate nexus approach to achieving SDGs and prevention/recovery.
As part of its knowledge dissemination efforts, the project carried out extensive communication and awareness campaigns to enhance visibility and strengthen stakeholder engagement on climate security challenges and resilience initiatives. These campaigns utilized a range of multimedia tools, including social media campaigns, radio spots, videos, and blog posts, targeting key audiences in Yemen, Iraq, Jordan, and Tunisia. The project actively engaged in 18 global and regional events to strengthen policy dialogue and stakeholder engagement. For example, at the 2023 Arab Forum for Sustainable Development, participants explored integrated approaches to climate action.
At MENA Climate Week 2023, discussions on the energy transition were informed by findings from regional reports. At COP28, the projects side events facilitated dialogue between policymakers and the private sector on accelerating climate finance for SDG aligned climate action. The Arab Future Energy Index (AFEX) Report also contributed to the global and regional stock take, informing the formulation of the first global stock take at COP28. Additionally, results from the SDG Climate Facility were communicated at UNCCD COP16, even though the project was concluded at that time, as it provided concrete examples of where desertification, drought, and climate action are integrated for effective response. These engagements expanded collaboration opportunities and facilitated discussions on innovative solutions. They further enabled engagement beyond regional and national institutions, expanding collaboration opportunities for a broader range of stakeholders.
The project also contributed to capacity development by implementing three rounds of a five day online training course on climate change mitigation, adaptation, and resilience, which targeted professionals from diverse sectors. One hundred twenty nine participants engaged in these sessions, and positive feedback was recorded in post training surveys. While some impacts of the project are still being measured, particularly those related to the integration of the climate security agenda nexus into main climate action plans (e.g., NDCs and NAPs), early signs of uptake are evident. Countries such as Yemen, Jordan, Iraq, Tunisia and Egypt are currently updating their national plans. Yemen received additional support from the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to start their NAP process, and Jordan recently received funding to update their NDC. Similarly, Egypt, Tunisia and Iraq are advancing their NDC updates. The project went beyond producing knowledge products, it also contributed to fostering policy dialogue on climate action and climate finance. In addition to the RCSN, the project strengthened two other regional networks: the Anticipatory Action Community of Practice and the Disaster Risk Reduction Partners Forum, both of which received support from the project. These networks facilitated the exchange of best practices and policy discussions among key regional actors.
The regional analysis of the Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action in the Arab States facilitated discussions on the role of finance ministries in climate interventions, aiming to improve coordination between ministries and establish a transparent system for NDC budget planning. While it has informed exchanges with institutions such as the IMF, World Bank, and UNEPFI. A key aspect of this effort was producing and disseminating several knowledge products designed to improve understanding of climate security risks and financing mechanisms. For example, the 2023 report Adapting to a New Climate in the MENA Region analyzed climate risks in the region, their economic implications, and banking sector responses. This report directly contributed to establishing a global working group of banks, enhanced the capacities of National Development and privately owned Banks, and focused on identifying opportunities for climate adaptation financing. Similarly, the Mobilizing Islamic Finance for Climate Action guide, developed in collaboration with the Islamic Development Bank and the General Council for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions, provided valuable insights into climate action within Islamic finance, potentially broadening financing mechanisms for climate resilience.
The project produced two AGIR technical reports, the first covering many topics to increase knowledge for deeper assessments in SDGs, Climate Vulnerabilities, Risk, Resilience, and Nexus. The second report compiled available information, emphasizing the need for a coherent GeoInformation System (GIS) and science based decision making tools. These reports contribute to developing a regional atlas on social vulnerability and aim to enhance communication, raise awareness, and support advocacy on climate hotspots in the Arab region. GIS maps were created for regions facing climatic risks, marking areas vulnerable to climate change impacts. These resources were integrated into the AGIR database and will inform future policy decisions, improving regional communication and awareness.
Outcome 3: National and local capacities to effectively integrate climate change considerations into development and crisis prevention/recovery policies and to scaleup climate finance for local innovative solutions with cobenefits across the SDGs. Through this outcome, the project sought to advance the integration of climate adaptation strategies and SDGs into development and crisis prevention/recovery policies by leveraging technical assistance and building (local) capacities across multiple countries in the MENA region.
This outcome also focused on implementing seven resilience grants in six different countries. Namely, Tunisia, Egypt, Yemen (Qat to Coffee, Waste to Energy), Iraq, Jordan, and Palestine. These grants supported local initiatives in sustainable energy, food security, climate finance, circular economy, and climate resilience. All countries under the resilience grants demonstrated catalysing effects on climate finance for further action and showcase replication and scaling up opportunities, whether from vertical funds such as the Green Climate Fund and the Global Environment Facility, bilateral donors, or the private sector. For instance, Yemens experience and lessons learned in transitioning from qat to coffee production were integrated into another UNDP/KfW project named Integrated Water Resource Management to Enhance the Resilience of Agriculture and Food Security and used for the proposal development of a GEF/ Least Development Countries Fund (LDCF) project titled Building climate resilience of livelihood systems in agriculture and water sectors in Abyn and Shabwah.
Another example is the resilience grant in Iraq, which received additional funding from Canada to accelerate efforts on green jobs through solar PV purification installations and the integration of nature based solutions to accelerate the climate security nexus in the Marshlands of Iraq. Furthermore, in the State of Palestine, despite the resilience grants nimble size, it catalyzed US$ $2.35 million in private finance through the effective derisking of investment for private sector solar developers, which allowed them to install centralized solar PV plants in two municipalities.
